title: Estimating and pricing
summary: How to turn a signed scope into an estimate you can defend, choose between fixed and hourly pricing, and plan for AI usage costs that grow with every click.
youWillLearn: How to estimate by breaking stories into small tasks with three numbers each
Which work Claude Code does not speed up, and why you need a buffer
When to use a fixed price and when to bill by the hour
How to estimate and contain AI usage costs before they surprise anyone

glossary.estimate: Your best forecast of the effort a piece of work will take, given as a range with the reasons behind it.
glossary.three-point estimate: Estimating each task three times, for the best case, the most likely case and the worst case, then combining the numbers.
glossary.buffer: Extra time added on top of an estimate for the problems you cannot see yet.
glossary.fixed price: One agreed amount for an agreed scope. If the work takes longer, the builder absorbs the extra hours.
glossary.time and materials: Billing for the hours actually worked, at an agreed rate. If the work takes longer, the client pays more.
glossary.milestone: A visible point in the project, like "booking works on staging", that is tied to a payment.
glossary.deposit: A payment made before work starts. It commits the client and covers your early work.
glossary.staging: A private copy of the app, separate from the live one, where changes are tested before real users see them.
glossary.token: The unit AI models read and write in, roughly a short word or part of a word. AI APIs bill per token.
glossary.pass-through: A running cost the client pays directly to the provider, from their own account, rather than through your invoice.
glossary.spend limit: A cap set in a provider's dashboard that stops or alerts on usage once monthly spending reaches an amount.

steps.title: Sam signed the scope. Now: the price
body: Sam owns a small hair salon. In discovery (the last lesson) you agreed on a one-page scope doc: online booking, text reminders and an owner calendar. She signed it.
You are the builder: you will make the app with Claude Code. Before you start, Sam needs to know what it will cost.

callout.text: New to this module? Lesson 1, Discovery and scoping, shows how Sam's vague wish became that one signed page.

scene.caption: Sam signed the scope doc you wrote. No price yet.

steps.title: "So, roughly how much?"
body: On the call Sam asks: "So, roughly how much?" You feel the pressure to say a number on the spot.
A number said out loud becomes the price in her head. Say a low figure today and a higher one next week, and you lose trust, even if the higher one was always right.

callout.text: A safe answer on the call: "I will send a written estimate within two days, with a range and what drives it." Clients trust a clear process more than a fast guess.

changes: + Arrow from Sam to You: "how much?"
~ You: put on the spot
~ Scope Doc fades back

scene.caption: Sam asks for a price. A number from your gut is a promise with nothing under it.

steps.title: Small tasks, three numbers each
body: Big things are hard to guess. Small things are easier. So split each Must story into tasks of half a day to two days, and give each task three numbers: best, likely and worst case.
This three-point estimate makes you think about what could go wrong. The widest gap shows where the risk lives.

code.caption: A spreadsheet does the same job. What matters is three honest numbers per task.

changes: − Sam, Scope Doc, You: we zoom into one story
+ Online Booking: one Must story from the scope
+ Slot Picker, Bookings Table, Booking Guard: its tasks
~ Estimate ? → 4.1 days for this story

scene.caption: One story, three small tasks. Each carries best / likely / worst days.

steps.title: The work that is not coding
body: Claude Code makes writing code faster. It does not speed up calls, waiting for feedback, reviewing what it wrote, testing on real phones or fixing deploys.
On small client projects that work is a large share of the hours. Give it its own lines, then add a buffer on top for the problems you cannot see yet.

callout.text: Ask Claude Code: "List everything needed to ship this story, including tests, migrations, env vars and deploy steps." Compare its list with yours. It tends to miss meetings, revision rounds and waiting time, because it never sees them.

changes: − Online Booking, Slot Picker, Bookings Table, Booking Guard
+ Coding, Testing, Calls: the three kinds of work
+ Buffer: extra time for problems you cannot see yet
~ Estimate 4.1 → 7 days

scene.caption: Coding got faster. Testing and calls did not. The buffer sits on top.

steps.title: Fixed price or hourly: who holds the risk
body: With a fixed price, Sam pays one agreed amount. If the work runs two days long, you pay for them in unpaid hours. With hourly billing, called time and materials, she pays for the hours worked.
Neither is better. Fixed price needs a tight, signed scope. Hourly fits fuzzy or changing work.

callout.text: A set menu versus ordering à la carte. With the set menu, the kitchen carries the risk of extra portions. À la carte, the guest pays for exactly what arrives.

changes: − Coding, Testing, Calls, Buffer
+ Sam and You, twice: once per pricing model
+ Two zones: Fixed price and Hourly

scene.caption: Same two-day overrun, different payer. The pricing model decides.

steps.title: A deposit and milestones
body: For a fixed price, split payment into milestones Sam can see: a deposit to start, a payment when booking works on staging (a private test copy of the app), the rest at launch.
The deposit commits Sam and pays for early work. Milestones keep both sides honest: nobody is more than one step out of pocket.

code.code:
Milestone                    Share  Trigger
1. Kickoff deposit            30%  contract signed
2. Booking flow on staging    40%  Sam tests the criteria
3. Launch + handoff           30%  live, docs delivered
code.caption: Example split. Tie each trigger to something Sam can check, not to "60% done".

changes: − Both pairs of Sam and You, and the two zones
+ Deposit, Staging Demo, Launch: three payments

scene.caption: Payments follow visible progress. Each step is small enough to trust.

steps.title: AI costs grow with every click
body: Say Sam later approves AI rebooking. The app server (the computer running the salon's code) sends each call to the Claude API, Anthropic's AI. It bills in tokens, in and out, at different rates.
Hosting stays flat; AI usage does not. Estimate it like a utility bill: calls × tokens × price, using the provider's price page.

code.caption: Show Sam a low, expected and high month. Usage, not your build, sets this number.

changes: − Deposit, Staging Demo, Launch
+ App Server and Claude API: the AI rebooking feature
+ Monthly Bill: grows with every call
~ AI calls 0 → 3,000 a month

scene.caption: Every AI click sends tokens in and out. The bill grows with usage.

steps.title: Let running costs pass through
body: Running costs belong to the client: hosting (the servers and database), text messages and AI. The clean setup is a pass-through: accounts in Sam's name, on her card, so she pays providers directly.
Your quote then has two parts: your fee for the build, and an estimated monthly running cost, as a range. Lesson 3 sets up those accounts.

callout.text: If you do pay a cost on the client's behalf, invoice it as a separate line with a margin you state openly. Hidden markups on usage turn into awkward conversations when usage spikes.

changes: ~ Monthly Bill → Sam's Card: she pays providers directly
+ Hosting: runs the app and database, billed monthly
+ SMS Service: sends the reminders, billed per text

scene.caption: Every running cost lands on Sam's card. Your invoice covers only your work.

steps.title: One bug can burn a month's budget
body: A bug that retries an AI call forever, or a bot hammering the feature, can spend a lot overnight. Under a fixed price, that bill becomes an argument.
Protect both sides: a spend limit in the provider's dashboard, a max_tokens cap (the longest reply allowed) on every call, a limit on retries, and a log of usage per call.

callout.text: When Claude Code writes an AI call, check: is max_tokens sized to the feature? Is the model id in one env var, not in five files? Does it log the usage numbers? Is there a retry cap and a rate limit in front of it?

changes: − Hosting, SMS Service
+ Retry Loop: a bug that calls the AI again and again
~ AI calls 3,000 → 300,000 a month
~ Sam's Card: a spend limit stops the damage

scene.caption: A runaway loop multiplies calls. The spend limit on Sam's card stops it.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Never price from your gut. Split stories into small tasks, give each three numbers, add the non-coding work and a buffer, and send a range in writing.
Fixed price puts the risk on you, so it needs a tight scope and milestones. Running costs, AI usage above all, pass through to the client and need caps from day one.
changes: − Retry Loop: fixed, with a retry cap
~ AI calls 300,000 → 3,000 a month

scene.caption: Calls back to normal, capped per call, and paid from Sam's own card.

quiz.question: Your estimate for a task is best 1 day, likely 1.5, worst 6. What does that tell you?

options.text: Use 1.5 days; the likely case is what usually happens.
options.why: Ignoring the worst case is how fixed-price projects lose money. The wide gap is information, not noise.

options.text: The task hides an unknown. Spike it or split it before you commit.
options.why: A gap that large means you do not understand part of the work yet. Learn more first, or price the risk in.
A plain average hides the problem. The point is to notice the risk and do something about it.

quiz.question: Sam's scope is still fuzzy, and she expects to change her mind as she sees screens. Which pricing fits best?

options.text: Fixed price, with a big buffer.
options.why: A fixed price on a moving scope turns every change into an argument, and the buffer will not be enough.

options.text: Free until she is happy, then one invoice.
options.why: That puts all the risk on you and gives Sam no reason to decide.

options.text: Time and materials, with a budget cap and regular check-ins.
options.why: Hourly billing fits changing work. The cap and check-ins keep Sam in control of the total.

quiz.question: Claude Code wrote an AI endpoint that retries on any error with no limit, and sets max_tokens far higher than the feature needs. What is the main risk for a client project?

options.why: Maybe, but that is not the expensive part.

options.text: A runaway bill if something loops or gets abused.
options.why: Unlimited retries and no output cap mean one bug or bot can multiply token usage. Add a retry limit, a sensible max_tokens, rate limiting and a spend limit.

options.text: The model may give a wrong answer.
options.why: That is a quality risk, but retries and missing caps are a cost risk.

takeaways: Never say a number on the first call. Send a written range with the reasons behind it.
Estimate small tasks with best, likely and worst cases. A wide gap means unknown work: spike it.
Claude Code speeds up coding, not calls, reviews or revisions. Estimate those separately, plus a buffer.
Fixed price moves the risk to you; protect it with a tight scope, a deposit and milestones.
AI usage is a running cost: estimate it per month, pass it through, and cap it with max_tokens and a spend limit.
